beats.intro: Learning module six. [[sub]]How futures are priced, and why their value behaves differently from forwards.
beats.inception: [[head]]At inception, a futures contract, like a forward, has a value of zero. [[eq]]With no income or costs, the futures price is the spot price grown at the risk-free rate. [[gold]]Gold at seventeen seventy, a two percent rate, and ninety-one days to maturity: [[ans]]the futures price is seventeen seventy-eight seventy-six an ounce. [[storage]]Add two dollars of storage, paid at maturity. Its present value is one ninety-nine, and the futures price rises to seventeen eighty seventy-eight.
beats.mtm: [[fwd]]Now follow the value over time. A forward's price is fixed, and its gains and losses pile up until maturity. [[ex]]Say seventy-one days pass and gold falls fifty dollars, to seventeen twenty. [[calc]]The forward's value is seventeen twenty minus the present value of seventeen seventy-eight seventy-six for the twenty days left: minus fifty-six eighty-three an ounce. A loss of five thousand six hundred eighty-three dollars, not yet paid. [[fut]]A futures contract never builds up a value like that. Every day, the gain or loss is paid through the margin account, and the value resets to zero.
beats.days: [[head]]Compare the two, day by day. [[d1]]Day one: the futures price falls five dollars. Procam pays five hundred dollars from its margin account, [[call]]drops below maintenance, and tops up five hundred. [[f1]]The forward has an unrealized loss of four ninety-eight an ounce. Nothing is paid. [[d2]]Day two: futures fall four more dollars. Procam pays four hundred, leaving four thousand five hundred fifty, above maintenance. [[f2]]The forward's unrealized loss grows to eight ninety-five an ounce. [[sum]]The cumulative results are about the same. But the futures loss is paid as it happens, and the forward's sits as counterparty credit risk until maturity.
beats.irfut: [[head]]Interest rate futures are a standardized, exchange-traded alternative to F R As. [[eq]]They are quoted as a price: one hundred minus the rate. [[ex]]A price of ninety-eight twenty-five means a three-month rate of one point seven five percent, three months from now. [[long]]A long futures position gains when the price rises, which means the rate falls. It is like lending. [[short]]A short position gains when rates rise, like borrowing. [[fra]]So a short futures position matches a long F R A, where you pay fixed.
beats.bpv: [[head]]Futures gains and losses are measured by the basis point value. [[eq]]Notional, times one basis point, times the period. [[ex]]For one million dollars of three-month rate, that is twenty-five dollars. [[dep]]A deposit at two point two one percent grows to one million five thousand five hundred twenty-five. [[up]]One basis point more adds twenty-five dollars; [[down]]one basis point less takes away twenty-five. The relationship is fixed and linear.
beats.baywhite: [[head]]Baywhite Financial made sixty-day fixed-rate loans, funded by borrowing at one-month M R R. [[risk]]Its risk: one-month M R R could be higher when it rolls its funding in a month. [[sell]]To hedge, it sells one-month rate futures on fifty million dollars. [[bpv]]The basis point value is fifty million times point oh one percent, times one twelfth: four hundred sixteen dollars sixty-seven. [[gain]]If it sells at ninety-eight seventy-five, and the contract settles at ninety-seven seventy-five, rates rose one hundred basis points. The gain is forty-one thousand six hundred sixty-seven dollars, offsetting its higher funding cost.
beats.diff: [[head]]Do forward and futures prices differ? [[same]]They are identical if interest rates are constant, or if futures prices and rates are uncorrelated. [[pos]]If futures prices rise when rates rise, a long futures position is better: gains are reinvested at higher rates, and losses are financed at lower rates. So futures prices are higher. [[neg]]If the correlation is negative, the long forward is preferred, and forward prices are higher. [[small]]For short maturities, the difference is usually tiny.
beats.convexity: [[head]]One exception is the convexity bias. Compare a long rate future with an F R A receiving fixed at two point two one percent, on one million dollars. [[fut]]The future pays exactly twenty-five dollars per basis point, in either direction. [[fra]]The F R A is settled at a present value, discounted at the new rate. So a twenty basis point fall pays four ninety-seven fifty, while a twenty basis point rise costs four ninety-seven oh one. [[chart]]The futures line is straight. The F R A line is slightly curved. That curvature is convexity, and it grows with longer discounting periods.
beats.clearing: [[head]]Finally, central clearing narrows the gap between futures and forwards. [[ccp]]Dealers must post margin to the central counterparty, [[users]]and they often require similar margin from their end-user clients. [[eff]]So O T C forwards now see futures-like cash flows. Users of both must keep enough cash or eligible collateral, and count the financing and administrative costs.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]At inception, futures and forward prices are both the spot price grown at the carry rate. [[w2]]Forward value builds until maturity; futures value is settled daily and resets to zero. [[w3]]Rate futures trade at one hundred minus the rate, with a fixed basis point value. [[w4]]Price differences come from rate correlation and convexity; central clearing narrows them.
beats.finish: That's the end of learning module six.
